anenefan · Nov 26, 2026

I do know the 2008 GFC hit the finances of the government hard, but I believe the ongoing culprit was more the expectation and pressure placed on the various departments to perform ... with a bean counter not too far away from decision making. During the 90s the Northern Central coast only iirc two inspectors for all the shipping coming into ports in the region.

Management plans are typically not the best plans, just a good fit for amount of effort, money and time.

The problem would have been better addressed IMO, as a firm eradication plan, temporary jobs, time driven where an acceptable secondary kill would be temporary, rather than a plan which allowed for ongoing funding if the current approach was not greatly successful. There is a temptation to turn a temporary job into a life long one if it pays well. I'm not familiar so much with Brisbane's fire ant eradication, but my guess is small wins were represented as having passed a significant mark in the program where it was then decided based on that, what remained didn't justify a great amount of funding.

Though in my region fire ant outbreaks at one of the hinterland coal mines have supposedly been dealt with, but I see the same sort of pussyfooting with the crazy yellow ant that was found in 2019 at Airlie Beach [1] and at the time could not fathom why a large response wasn't happening given how poorly Brisbane's fire ant eradication had been. Just imagine my surprise to find out further south down the coast, recently found they too have crazy yellow ants. [2]

Jedd · Nov 28, 2026

We (AU) got varroa mite - that's the one that's likely responsible for honeybee colony collapse most other places on the planet - 4 years ago. There was a year of concerted effort to track, trace, and destroy hives & nests wherever it was found, but after a year or so we moved to a 'management' phase, which was sad, but likely inevitable.

We think this arrived somewhere in NSW, and tracing certainly suggests that.

Latest (maybe a month ago) that I heard was the rise of treatment-resistant mites, which should have taken a lot longer to appear, suggest varroa may have been with us for a while before that (though obviously almost no one would have been using those treatments during that intervening time ... or would they?).

Point being, AU's coast is huge, and the number of international ports is non-trivial, and like everywhere else, we have a surfeit of idiots.

One of our primary detection systems for varroa were sentinel beehives maintained near the various ports, and frequently checked for pests. The bait program is probably a similar prophylactic (I'm speculating) and likely one of a range of detection programmes in place.

(For varroa, it didn't help us as it looks like a bee package was imported directly, rather than accidentally catching a ride on a container ship.)
